title: Single strand vs doubled thread
subtitle: Choosing how many strands to put on the needle and why it matters.
excerpt: The number of strands on the needle changes the weight and coverage of every stitch. Too few strands leaves the cloth showing through; too many strands makes the surface lumpy and hard to pull through.
sourceNotes:
Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. Strand separation and thread weight guidance.
Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), Internet Archive. Thread weight and fabric coverage notes.

glossaryTerms.definition: The number of individual strands of stranded cotton placed on the needle for a particular piece of work. Standard six-strand thread is typically split to two strands for 14-count Aida cross-stitch.
How fully the thread fills a stitch so the ground cloth does not show through. Correct coverage depends on matching strand count to cloth count.

content.text: The
strand count

is one of the first decisions for any embroidery or cross-stitch project. Get it right and the cloth looks fully covered, the back lies flat, and the needle moves freely. Get it wrong and you are fighting the work for the rest of the piece.
Standard strand counts by cloth
These are the defaults. A pattern may call for something different, but these counts give correct
fabric coverage
in the absence of a specific instruction.
11-count Aida: three strands. The larger holes need more thread to fill.
14-count Aida: two strands. The most common combination; the default for beginners.
16-count Aida or 28-count evenweave stitched over two threads: two strands.
18-count Aida or 32-count evenweave stitched over two threads: one strand for fine detail; two strands for fuller coverage on a visible piece.
36 to 40-count linen stitched over two threads: one strand. Fine miniature work.
How to separate strands
Cut a length of stranded cotton, about 40 to 50 cm.
Hold the cut length at the centre between two fingers. Let the two halves hang down.
Take one strand at the top of one end between thumb and forefinger and pull it slowly and smoothly upward, away from the rest. The other strands will bunch and then drop back smoothly.
Repeat until you have the number of strands you need. Lay them together on the needle rather than threading them one at a time.
Single strand uses

A single strand suits fine blackwork lines, backstitch outlines on finished cross-stitch, and surface embroidery that needs a crisp edge. One strand also allows subtle shading in needlepainting where threads of different colours are blended.
Common mistakes

attrs.heading: What goes wrong
attrs.intro: Strand count problems and how to recognise them.

items.symptom: The cloth shows through between stitches
items.cause: Too few strands for the cloth count, or the stitches are not sitting flat in the holes.
items.fix: Add one more strand and stitch a test square. If coverage improves, continue. Also check that each half of a cross-stitch is sitting flat before the second leg is worked.

items.symptom: The thread is hard to pull through the cloth
items.cause: Too many strands for the cloth count or needle size.
items.fix: Reduce by one strand, or move up one needle size so the eye creates a larger channel through the cloth.

content.text: What this underpins
Strand count matters in every needlework discipline, from cross-stitch to surface embroidery and Hardanger. The choices in this guide apply across all sub-categories.
